slides.title: Real-World Problems and Significant Digits
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q3 and Q4 are today's two tools. Q3 asks which digits are there at all — the zero between the 9 and the 2 survives the conversion, and that is exactly the zero that counts. Q4 asks how to stop at a named place, which is what every answer today ends with. Say at the reveal: today you will decide where to stop, and then stop there.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Four rules, one table. Every nonzero digit counts. A zero between nonzero digits counts — it is holding a place that was measured. A leading zero never counts; it is only saying where the decimal point is. A trailing zero counts only when a decimal point is written, because writing 3.200 is a claim about the thousandths and writing 52,000 is not.
OFF: 'Scientific notation makes this easy. In 5.2 times ten to the fourth, every digit you can see is significant — that is one of the reasons the notation exists.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
An answer cannot be more precise than the worst measurement that went into it. Count the significant digits in each measurement and give the answer the smaller count. Do the arithmetic in full first and round once, at the end — rounding early loses digits that the arithmetic still needed.
OFF: 'Two significant digits in, two significant digits out. The answer is never better than the measurement it came from.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
This is the rule almost everyone gets wrong, textbooks included. For a sum or a difference you do not count digits — you look at WHERE each measurement's last digit sits, and the answer stops at the leftmost of those places. 1,234 stops at the ones place; 5.6 stops at the tenths; so the sum stops at the ones place. Counting digits instead would give 1.2 times ten cubed, which throws away two digits that were actually measured.
OFF: 'Products count digits. Sums count places. They are two different rules and it matters which one you reach for.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Ask for the significant-digit count of each measurement before anyone multiplies. The count decides the answer's shape, and knowing it first stops the class from rounding in the middle.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Multiply in full — 10,750 — and round once. 1.25 has three significant digits and 8.6 has two, so the answer keeps two. A board with 1.075 × 10⁴ did the arithmetic and skipped the question; a board with 1.0 × 10⁴ rounded 10,750 down instead of up.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Same shape, the counts the other way round. 460 · 235 = 108,100, and the two-digit measurement is the first one this time. Catches 1.081 × 10⁵ (not rounded) and 1.08 × 10⁵ (rounded to three).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Ask where each measurement's last digit sits before anything is subtracted. This is the item the book gets wrong, and the place question is the whole of it.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Subtract in full, then stop at the leftmost last-digit place. 0.00309 stops at the hundred-thousandths; 0.00003472 stops eight places out. The leftmost of the two is the hundred-thousandths, so that is where the answer stops. A board with 3.05528 × 10⁻³ never rounded; a board with 3.1 × 10⁻³ rounded one place too far — here counting digits would also have given 3.06 × 10⁻³, which is why the book never noticed its rule was wrong.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 3,850 stops at the tens place and 274 stops at the ones, so the answer stops at the tens. The rounding bites: 3,576 becomes 3,580. A board with 3.576 × 10³ did the subtraction and skipped the question.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: All four rules in one number. The two leading zeros never count; the 4 and the 7 do; the trailing zero counts because a decimal point is written. A board with 2 dropped the trailing zero, and that zero is the whole point of writing it.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: The place rule, and it costs a lot here: 2,500 stops at the hundreds place, so a sum of 2,971 has to be reported as 3,000. Students hate this one and they are right to — it is telling them the truth about what was measured. A board with 2.971 × 10³ skipped the rounding; a board with 3.0 × 10³ has it.

slides.note: A quotient that comes out exact and still has to be cut. 4.20 has three significant digits and 3.0 has two, so the answer keeps two: 140. Writing 140 with no decimal point is the honest two-digit form, and 1.4 × 10² says it without ambiguity — which is the argument for the notation.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and it is the exit evidence. Ellis has used the multiply-and-divide rule on an addition. Full credit: the rule for a sum is about the place where each measurement's last digit sits, not the number of digits; 1,234 stops at the ones place and 5.6 at the tenths, so the sum stops at the ones place; 1,239.6 becomes 1,240. A student who only writes 'he used the wrong rule' has not said what the right one is.
